 Scott Morrow making the most of his chance in Rangers lineup with Sean Durzi out 
 By 
 Andrew Crane 
 Published 
 Nov. 14, 2026, 9:51 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. 
 Make New York Post a Preferred Source 
 By the end of the sequence, when Alexis Lafrenière flew across the crease and tucked a goal into the Canucks net Friday, Scott Morrow’s contribution flew under the radar. But at the other end of the ice, late in the second period of the Rangers’ eventual 5-1 win , Morrow — one of the final players on the roster out of training camp who watched the first 14 games from the press box — managed to back-check the puck away from Brendan Gallagher, with both of his knees hitting the ice, to start the rush. 
 To Tom Upton, the Brown men’s ice hockey head coach who was an assistant at UMass during Morrow’s final two seasons there, moments like that capture urgency in a game. And for Morrow, the 24-year-old whose brief career to this point has relied on patience, his latest Rangers chance has been full of it. With Sean Durzi out the past seven games with an undisclosed injury, Morrow went from not playing at all to becoming a contributor on the blue line while playing alongside rookie Alberts Smits and Matthew Robertson.

 His window of opportunity might be fleeting. Durzi, who skated on the second pairing before his injury, will return eventually, and Braden Schneider — on the third pairing — has been a staple in the lineup for years. But Morrow’s play and contributions will make it difficult for head coach Mike Sullivan to take him out of the lineup, with his plus-3 mark evidence of that. 
 “Three, four years ago, maybe he doesn’t come back on that puck as hard and come into his zone as hard,” Upton told The Post on Saturday after hearing about Morrow’s back-check. “But he knows he needs to continue to do those little things to stay at that level and compete at that level, so that adds to that urgency, right?” 
 The strong contributions from Morrow have also validated the Blueshirts decision to keep eight defensemen out of training camp and avoid the gamble of losing Morrow on waivers. He was part of the return in the K’Andre Miller trade in July 2025 after logging 16 games with the Hurricanes — and plenty of time in the AHL — following his entry-level deal. Morrow, Upton said, has always been a skilled defenseman offensively, but over his three seasons with the Minutemen, including the final two with Upton on staff, he worked on the stick details, angles and checking that would add defensive value to his game. 
 Scott Morrow (60) of the New York Rangers skates during an NHL game against the Edmonton Oilers in Edmonton, Alberta, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. NHLI via Getty Images 
 Morrow’s ability to create space for himself and create offense for others led to him collecting six goals and 30 minutes during his final UMass season in 2023-24, 13 goals in his first AHL season the following year and another five goals — and 19 points — across 34 games with AHL Hartford last year. But after the Rangers overhauled their second pairing on the blue line with the arrivals of Durzi and Marcus Pettersson, and after they selected Smits at No. 5 overall, Morrow was staring down a complicated path. He skated in 29 games last year during a lost Blueshirts season, but the organization suddenly had a logjam at the position. 
 Even after the Rangers kept him, though, Morrow needed to be patient again. It took Durzi’s absence to finally create an opening in the lineup.

 “None of us want our guys on the sidelines for any extended period of time,” Sullivan said earlier this month. “That’s not an easy circumstance.” 
 Entering Monday’s game against the Canadiens at the Garden, Morrow has maximized his chance, though. Against the Oilers on Nov. 1, Morrow skated toward the net off a faceoff, sent a shot and watched as Pavel Dorofeyev turned the rebound into a goal. Sullivan said Saturday that Morrow “has been very effective joining the rush, helping us off the offensive blue line.” 
 It took Morrow more than a month to get his first opportunity at making a first impression. It hasn’t led to clarity about his role moving forward, but after being on the roster bubble, he has started to flash some of the potential that shaped his rise as a valued blue-line prospect in the first place. 
 “I don’t make those decisions that the higher-ups do at the NHL level,” Upton said of keeping Morrow out of training camp to avoid waivers, “but for me, if you’re gonna have a guy that’s gonna be in a seventh or eighth defenseman role and a little bit of a development role on your roster, why wouldn’t you take the kid that does things with the puck that you can’t teach and does things that other people can’t?
 “I’m not shocked to see that decision by them, and obviously, it seems like it’s working out well and he’s progressing well.”
